finding.title: Overstated fidelity claim that current movement-cancellation 'matches' the GDD's interruption rule
finding.description: door-open-interaction's repository_evidence for PlayerInteractionController.cs states that 'EndInteraction is also called on any player movement and on PlayerHealth.Damaged, matching the GDD's interruption rules for movement/damage.' This slightly overstates the match: the GDD's rule is specifically that, once the auto-timer has started, 'moving away' cancels progress while cursor drift after the initial click does not — a distinction that presupposes the cursor-targeted click-to-approach model. The current WASD-polling implementation has no cursor-target concept at all and cancels on any movement input (Update() checks input magnitude, not actual displacement or direction relative to the door), which is a coarser trigger than the GDD's 'moving away' condition. The observation's wording could be read as certifying behavioral equivalence with the required interruption semantics rather than mere superficial similarity (both involve movement-triggered cancellation). This does not change the item's correct 'partial' repository_state, since the item is already flagged as missing the entire click-to-approach/cursor-drift-tolerant model.

gdd_evidence.requirement: Once the timer has begun, taking damage, moving away, or issuing another command that cancels/replaces the door interaction resets progress; cursor movement away from the selected door after the initial click does not reset progress.

repository_evidence.observation: OnPlayerMoved() unconditionally calls EndInteraction() whenever PlayerMovement reports any WASD input magnitude above threshold, with no concept of cursor drift vs. moving away, and no distinction based on direction relative to the door.

finding.recommended_change: Rephrase the evidence observation to state that the current any-movement-cancels behavior is only superficially similar to the GDD's movement-interruption rule, and explicitly note that it does not yet implement the required cursor-drift-tolerant distinction because no cursor-targeting model exists in the current code.

finding.title: gameplay-navigation-locomotion may be over-classified as needs_execution_decomposition; its stated reason double-counts an already-extracted prerequisite
finding.description:
`gameplay-navigation-locomotion` is marked `needs_execution_decomposition` with the reason that it bundles three things: (1) "consuming/validating the newly configured AI Navigation package", (2) adding NavMesh-capable walkability configuration to builder-generated scene geometry, and (3) designing/implementing the shared passability interface.

Responsibility (1) is not work owned by this item at all — package declaration/resolution was already extracted into `tilemap-navigation-package-configuration` (single_agent), and this item already carries a `depends_on` edge to it. Merely consuming a satisfied prerequisite is not an independently verifiable implementation responsibility, so the execution_reason inflates the apparent breadth.

What actually remains is (2) NavMesh walkability configuration over a very small existing geometry set, and (3) a small semantic-state-to-walkability interface with four enumerated states. The GDD explicitly scopes this item as "A minimal working navigation/locomotion layer" that must exist before locomotion-dependent enemy work is dispatched, and explicitly leaves the underlying Unity mechanism (obstacle/carving, navigation link, or runtime navigation-data update) as an implementation choice rather than a design decision. That combination reads as a bounded one-agent unit with a clear validation target (the item's own criterion: toggling each of sealed/open/locked/broken produces the correct walkability result).

This matters disproportionately because this node is the highest-fanout blocker in the graph: `enemy-pursuit-search-foundation`, `enemy-status-effect-displacement`, and `door-close-lock-break-lifecycle` all depend on it directly, and everything enemy-side and door-lifecycle-side depends on it transitively. Leaving it in a state that requires a Progressive Decomposer pass before anything downstream can move is a real cost if the item is in fact already one agent's work.

I am not asserting the classification is definitely wrong — a reviewer could reasonably argue the passability interface is a cross-domain contract worth isolating. I am asserting the stated reason does not currently support the classification.

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §5 — 2.5D Isometric Visual and World Representation
gdd_evidence.requirement: "The approved enemy-navigation implementation is Unity AI Navigation (com.unity.ai.navigation) using NavMesh-based runtime movement. A minimal working navigation/locomotion layer and the approved package configuration must exist before locomotion-dependent enemy implementation is dispatched, but room-specific visual authoring does not need to be complete first."

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §3 — Door and Pursuit Rules (Door passability contract)
gdd_evidence.requirement: "The exact Unity mechanism used beneath this interface (for example obstacle/carving, a navigation link, or runtime navigation-data update) is an implementation choice rather than a separate game-design decision."

repository_evidence.observation: The entire walkable geometry that would need navigation configuration today is produced by BuildFloor (one primitive Plane), BuildWalls (two primitive Cubes), and BuildDoor (one DoorRoot cube) — a very small surface for a NavMesh walkability pass, not a large scene-rework.

com.unity.ai.navigation is absent, which is precisely the gap already owned by the separate single_agent item `tilemap-navigation-package-configuration` that this item depends on — so package configuration is not additional scope inside this item.

finding.recommended_change: Either (a) re-classify `gameplay-navigation-locomotion` as `single_agent`, scoped explicitly to the GDD's "minimal working navigation/locomotion layer" (NavMesh walkability over the existing prototype geometry plus the sealed/open/locked/broken passability interface), or (b) keep `needs_execution_decomposition` but rewrite `execution_reason` so it no longer counts consumption of the already-extracted package-configuration prerequisite as one of the bundled responsibilities, and instead names the two genuinely separable responsibilities a decomposer should split.

finding.title: enemy-pursuit-search-foundation is one cohesive finite-state component; needs_execution_decomposition may be over-classification of a clean one-agent unit
finding.description:
`enemy-pursuit-search-foundation` is marked `needs_execution_decomposition` because it "bundles several independently verifiable responsibilities — detection acquisition, distance-based target loss, last-known-position homing, bounded randomized search/wander, reacquisition, doorway-passability-aware traversal, and restart-reset participation."

Those are states and transitions of a single finite-state machine over a single piece of state (the enemy's current target/last-known-position), not independently ownable systems. The GDD itself describes them as one artifact: "finite-state components control pursuit, attacks, target loss, search, and reacquisition across the floor's spaces." There is no enemy code in the repository at all, so this is a greenfield single component with no integration surface to reconcile against beyond the navigation layer it already depends on. Splitting a single FSM across agents would likely produce a worse handoff than keeping it whole, because each partial owner would need the same state contract in context.

The graph consequence is worth surfacing: this node is the sole gateway for all enemy work, and it is itself blocked by `gameplay-navigation-locomotion`, which is also `needs_execution_decomposition` (see ES-001). `melee-enemy` and `ranged-enemy` downstream are also `needs_execution_decomposition`. That produces a three-deep chain of decomposition-required nodes before any enemy behavior can be dispatched.

I flag this as a review item rather than an error: the acceptance-criteria volume (eight criteria) is genuinely high, and a reviewer could reasonably keep the current call. The direction of the risk is delay, not unsafe dispatch, so it does not block bootstrap.

gdd_evidence.requirement: "Once that shared navigation layer exists, finite-state components control pursuit, attacks, target loss, search, and reacquisition across the floor's spaces."

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §3 — Enemy Detection, Pursuit, and Target Loss
gdd_evidence.requirement: Detection/pursuit/target-loss/search/reacquisition are described as one continuous behavior over one target state, with only "Exact Detection Distance, Lose Target Distance, search duration, and search/wander weighting" deferred as tuning values.

repository_evidence.observation: Contains only Door/Player/Camera/UI scripts (DoorInteractable.cs, PlayerInteractionController.cs, PlayerMovement.cs, PlayerHealth.cs, PlayerMana.cs, PlayerManaUI.cs, IsometricCameraFollow.cs, and two debug controls). No enemy script exists, so this item is greenfield with no existing enemy integration surface for an agent to reconcile against.

finding.recommended_change: Re-examine whether `enemy-pursuit-search-foundation` should be `single_agent` as a single FSM component (attack behavior and archetype assembly already correctly excluded to the archetype items). If it is retained as `needs_execution_decomposition`, state in `execution_reason` which boundary a decomposer should cut along (for example: acquire/pursue/lose-target core versus bounded search-wander and reacquisition), rather than listing FSM states as if each were a separately ownable responsibility.

finding.title: melee-enemy and ranged-enemy absorb character presentation/prefab authoring that the GDD assigns to the reusable visual-world foundation
finding.description:
Both archetype items carry an acceptance criterion to "deliver a usable assembled world-space SpriteRenderer archetype prefab" following "isometric sorting conventions", and both cite that presentation work in their `execution_reason` as one of the responsibilities that makes them too large for one handoff.

But the GDD assigns character presentation to the reusable visual-world foundation, not to the archetype: "Character presentation is therefore part of the reusable visual-world foundation rather than a separate rendering architecture." `world-visual-foundation`'s own acceptance criteria already claim exactly this — that "the wizard, enemies, doors, props, obstacles ... use world-space SpriteRenderer prefabs ... following consistent isometric sorting conventions."

So the sorting/presentation conventions the archetypes are required to follow are owned by a different item that is neither a represented prerequisite of the archetypes nor explicitly excluded from their scope. The result is an ambiguous execution boundary: a future decomposer cannot tell whether the archetype owner is expected to establish sorting conventions itself, or to consume conventions that `world-visual-foundation` must produce first.

This is a boundary problem, not a request to redesign dependencies — I am reporting that the archetype's execution scope currently overlaps another owner's declared scope, which is one of the stated reasons those items were marked `needs_execution_decomposition`. Removing the overlap may materially change what the decomposition should look like.

Relatedly, the candidate's own `unresolved_questions[0]` acknowledges it does not yet know whether archetype validation requires instantiating enemy prefabs through `DoorPrototypeSceneBuilder.cs` and therefore whether the builder/scene exclusive locks apply. That uncertainty compounds the same boundary gap.

gdd_evidence.requirement: "World-space SpriteRenderer prefabs will be used for sealed doors, tall props, obstacles, the wizard, enemies, and other independently sorted or interactive objects. Character presentation is therefore part of the reusable visual-world foundation rather than a separate rendering architecture."

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §3 — Environment Presentation and Authoring Direction
gdd_evidence.requirement: "The reusable Tilemap/SpriteRenderer world foundation establishes authoring conventions and visual/gameplay separation; it does not by itself include authoring all five room layouts or encounter content" — i.e. the foundation owns conventions, while content/room authoring is what is excluded from it.

repository_evidence.observation: BuildFloor/BuildWalls/BuildDoor create primitive meshes with MeshRenderers; no SpriteRenderer, Tilemap, or sorting configuration exists anywhere in the builder, so no isometric sorting convention currently exists for an archetype task to follow.
No SpriteRenderer-based character or prop objects are serialized in the canonical scene; the player and door visuals are primitive MeshRenderer objects.

finding.recommended_change: In `melee-enemy` and `ranged-enemy`, state explicitly that the archetype consumes the isometric sorting/presentation conventions owned by `world-visual-foundation` rather than establishing them, and drop "SpriteRenderer prefab presentation/sorting" from the list of responsibilities cited as making the item oversized. Record for the later decomposer that the intended split is behavior/integration assembly versus presentation, with presentation gated on the visual foundation.

finding.title: Room-content-dependent validation is attached to foundation items as if currently executable
finding.description:
Several items claim room-specific validation targets that cannot run, because `five-room-content-authoring` is `needs_future_decomposition` and no named room exists in the repository:

- `enemy-pursuit-search-foundation` — validation_requirement: "Bone Archive lane-pathing validation confirming enemy movement/navigation fits the room's described narrow-lane geometry." Unqualified.
- `ranged-enemy` — validation_requirement: "Chapel of Ash line-of-sight/projectile-occlusion Play Mode validation confirming cover blocks shots." Unqualified.
- `encounter-admission-cap-enforcement` — its `execution_reason` positively asserts "a clear validation target (Lower Vault priority case) that does not require full room content to be authored", while its validation_requirement describes the Lower Vault case concretely as a rear breach coinciding with that room's own encounter admission request.

By contrast, `gameplay-navigation-locomotion` handles the identical situation correctly: its Bone Archive validation is explicitly annotated "this check becomes fully executable once Bone Archive content is authored, but the navigation layer's agent-radius/walkability configuration is the artifact being validated." That is the pattern the other three should follow.

The correct fix is annotation, not broadening: none of these tasks should acquire ownership of deferred room content merely so a future room-specific check can eventually run. The risk today is that an implementation agent accepts a task whose stated done-condition it cannot satisfy.

gdd_evidence.requirement: Bone Archive, Chapel of Ash, and Lower Vault are named authored spaces with specific tactical geometry (narrow lanes/chokepoints; pews and columns providing line-of-sight breaks; incomplete loops with a rear doorway to watch).

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §5 — 2.5D Isometric Visual and World Representation
gdd_evidence.requirement: "The reusable visual world foundation ... is distinct from authoring the five named room layouts and encounters. Five-room visual/content authoring consumes this foundation once it exists."

repository_evidence.observation: The only authored space is the generic single-door prototype room (Floor plane, two wall cubes, one DoorRoot); no Bone Archive, Chapel of Ash, or Lower Vault geometry exists, so none of the cited room-specific checks can execute today.

finding.recommended_change: Annotate the Bone Archive, Chapel of Ash, and Lower Vault validation requirements on these three items as checks that become executable once the corresponding room content exists, naming the mechanism actually under test now (pathing/agent-radius configuration, occlusion-check logic, admission arithmetic). Correct `encounter-admission-cap-enforcement`'s `execution_reason` so it does not claim the Lower Vault scenario is a presently-achievable validation target. Do not expand any of these items to own room content.

finding.title: single_agent spell and status-effect items carry acceptance-adjacent validation that requires unbuilt enemy archetypes
finding.description:
Four items marked `single_agent` state validation requirements that can only be exercised against enemy archetypes that do not exist and are not represented as prerequisites:

- `fireball` — "Validate that a full charge produces meaningful area damage against multiple naturally-clustering pursuing Melee Enemies" and "Validate that a tap shot remains usable against a Ranged Enemy's telegraphed attack pattern." Depends only on `player-movement` and `enemy-health-damage-defeat`.
- `frost-field` — "Validate that casting Frost Field creates a readable opening against a melee group (stretches pursuit)."
- `force-wave` — "Validate Force Wave functions as an effective emergency response against a surrounding melee cluster ... and confirm its short range makes it ineffective against distant Ranged Enemy pressure."
- `enemy-status-effect-displacement` — "Verify a Ranged Enemy under active Frost slowdown continues executing its telegraphed attack on schedule while only its repositioning speed is reduced." Depends only on `enemy-pursuit-search-foundation` and `gameplay-navigation-locomotion`; `ranged-enemy` is not a prerequisite.

Each item's *acceptance* surface is genuinely satisfiable through the interfaces it already depends on (mana spend exists; pointer/restriction, damage, and displacement interfaces are represented as prerequisites). The problem is the validation claim, which asserts a broader integration than the handoff can complete.

Note this is the pattern the retry-hardening guidance calls out specifically for enemy-status-effect-displacement: the Ranged-Enemy-attack-unaffected rule is a correctly-preserved acceptance constraint, but the *verification* of it against a live Ranged Enemy is a downstream integration check, not something this bounded component can run.

gdd_evidence.requirement: Melee Enemy and Ranged Enemy are the two required archetypes; the Ranged Enemy "keeps moderate distance and fires a slow telegraphed shot" — the behavior these validation claims exercise.
"Frost Field slows a ranged enemy's repositioning but does not stop its attacks" — a cross-system outcome observable only when both the status-effect owner and the Ranged Enemy archetype exist.

repository_evidence.observation: No enemy archetype script or prefab exists anywhere under Assets/, so no Melee or Ranged Enemy is available to any of these four tasks at validation time.

finding.recommended_change: Mark these archetype-dependent checks as validation that becomes executable once `melee-enemy`/`ranged-enemy` exist, and keep each item's presently-runnable validation target explicit (mana spend and refusal, restriction request/release, pointer-target consumption, displacement/slowdown apply-and-restore against a test double, reset and suspend entry points). Keep the items `single_agent`; do not broaden them and do not add archetype dependencies solely to make a future check runnable.

finding.title: door-open-interaction omits the shared Input Actions asset lock that every sibling input-touching task holds
finding.description:
`door-open-interaction` is correctly sized as `single_agent`, but its `exclusive_resources` list covers only DoorInteractable.cs, PlayerInteractionController.cs, the scene builder, and the canonical scene. It does not include `repo-file:Assets/InputSystem_Actions.inputactions`, even though one of its own acceptance criteria requires that "Door selection/approach input is consumed through the project's Unity Input System/Input Actions layer rather than independent direct hardware polling", and the work replaces a raw `Keyboard.current[interactKey]` read with cursor-targeted selection.

`player-movement`, `fireball`, `frost-field`, and `force-wave` all take that lock. The candidate's own `unresolved_questions[1]` states it cannot determine whether door selection needs its own binding or purely consumes a Point/Click binding that Player Movement will add. Under that acknowledged uncertainty, omitting the lock is the unsafe default: if door work does add a Player-map binding while a spell task is concurrently editing the same asset, two agents write the same non-merge-safe shared asset, which the GDD forbids outright.

I verified the underlying repository fact: the `Player` action map contains Move/Look/Attack/Interact/Crouch/Jump/Previous/Next/Sprint only. Point and Click exist solely in the separate `UI` map. So no existing gameplay binding satisfies cursor-targeted door selection today, which makes the "it will add a binding" branch the likely one.

This is purely a concurrency-metadata issue — the task size itself is fine and should stay `single_agent`.

gdd_evidence.requirement: "Tasks that depend on unfinished work, or that require changes to the same scripts, scenes, or prefabs, are completed sequentially. Agents do not modify the same Unity assets concurrently."

"Clicking a sealed door requests movement to its interaction position" and runtime input is "supplied through Unity Input System/Input Actions rather than independent direct hardware polling inside gameplay systems."

repository_evidence.observation: The 'Player' action map (from line 5) defines only Move, Look, Attack, Interact, Crouch, Jump, Previous, Next, Sprint. 'Point' and 'Click' appear only inside the separate 'UI' map (from line 479), so no gameplay cursor-selection binding currently exists.

Update() reads `Keyboard.current[interactKey]` directly (lines 30-44) and drives BeginInteraction/EndInteraction from that hold, confirming this task must replace hardware polling with Input Actions routing.

finding.recommended_change: Add `repo-file:Assets/InputSystem_Actions.inputactions` to `door-open-interaction`'s `exclusive_resources`, with the reason recorded as conservative sequencing under the open question about whether door selection adds its own binding or consumes Player Movement's. Keep `execution_scope: single_agent` unchanged — this is a lock, not a size problem.

finding.title: windows-build-scene-registration includes an acceptance criterion an agent likely cannot deliver as a committed change
finding.description:
`windows-build-scene-registration` is correctly `single_agent` for the GDD-backed work: registering the canonical gameplay scene in `ProjectSettings/EditorBuildSettings.asset`, which currently holds `m_Scenes: []`. The retry-hardening guidance explicitly supports this call — the required developer inspection before merge is a validation gate, not the task's execution scope.

However, the item adds a second acceptance criterion not present in the GDD text it cites: "Windows Standalone is configured as the active/target build platform." The active build target is Unity editor-user state (`Library/EditorUserBuildSettings.asset`), and this repository's `.gitignore` excludes `/[Ll]ibrary/` (line 9) and `/[Uu]ser[Ss]ettings/` (line 15). If that is where the setting lives, an agent cannot durably deliver or repo-verify it, and the item's stated validation target is partially unreachable even though the task is otherwise a clean one-agent unit.

The GDD's own requirement is narrower and fully deliverable: the canonical scene "must be registered in Unity Build Settings before the Windows delivery requirement can be considered complete."

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §5 — Approved Unity Packages and Windows Build Configuration
gdd_evidence.requirement: "The required delivery target is a Windows Standalone build. The current canonical gameplay scene is Assets/NoSafeCircle/DoorPrototype/Scenes/DoorPrototype.unity; that scene (or a later human-approved replacement canonical gameplay scene) must be registered in Unity Build Settings ... Package-manifest and ProjectSettings changes authorized by these approved requirements may be implemented by an agent, but the developer must inspect the resulting package state, scene registration, and Windows build configuration before merge."

repository_evidence.observation: Contains m_Scenes: [] — the scene-registration half of this item is a real, committable, agent-deliverable change.

Lines 9 and 15 exclude /[Ll]ibrary/ and /[Uu]ser[Ss]ettings/, where Unity stores active-build-target editor-user state; that portion of the acceptance criterion is therefore not representable as a committed repository change.

finding.recommended_change: Keep `execution_scope: single_agent`. Move "Windows Standalone is configured as the active/target build platform" out of the agent acceptance criteria and into the item's validation requirements alongside the already-recorded developer-inspection gate, or restate it as the committable portion (Windows player settings in ProjectSettings) if that is what was intended.

finding.title: Restart orchestrator depends on reset entry points that the named owners are not required to expose
finding.description:
Both restart items consume owner-controlled reset entry points, and the graph correctly routes those edges to concrete owners. However, two of the named owners carry no acceptance criterion requiring them to expose the reset entry point their dependent invokes.

`floor-run-restart-bootstrap` depends on `door-open-interaction` with the stated reason "DoorInteractable.cs already owns run-persistent state (Progress, IsOpen, disabled doorwayBlocker) but exposes no reset entry point; the bootstrap orchestrator must invoke one." `door-open-interaction`'s five acceptance criteria cover click-to-approach selection, arm's-reach auto-timer, cursor-drift tolerance, interruption, and Input System routing — none require a reset entry point. `floor-run-restart-persistent-closure` repeats the same dependency with the same expectation.

`floor-run-restart-persistent-closure` depends on `encounter-admission-cap-enforcement` because "Encounter activation/admission state is a named required reset participant." That item's three acceptance criteria cover registry query, delay/reduce-first admission, and non-duplication of the count — none require a reset entry point.

Every other named persistent owner in the graph does carry the reset criterion (`player-health`, `player-mana`, `player-movement`, `doorway-crossing-state`, `door-close-lock-break-lifecycle`, `active-enemy-registry`, `enemy-health-damage-defeat`, `enemy-pursuit-search-foundation`, `enemy-status-effect-displacement`, `fireball`, `frost-field`, `force-wave`), so the gap is specific and inconsistent rather than a deliberate staging choice. As written, both owner items can be implemented, validated, and closed while leaving the restart items' dependencies unsatisfiable — the requirement exists only inside the consumer's `depends_on.reason`, which is not an owner obligation.

gdd_evidence.requirement: "Every system that owns state that can persist or remain active when restart occurs must expose a reset entry point for the state it owns, and the orchestrator invokes those owned reset interfaces. Required reset participants include ... door lifecycle/crossing/durability state, and encounter activation/admission state."
"Restart resets all run-persistent gameplay state to the floor's initial state, including ... door lifecycle/crossing/durability state, and encounter activation/admission state."

"It invokes reset entry points owned by each stateful system rather than directly mutating their internals ... door lifecycle/crossing/durability state, and encounter activation/admission state must all participate once those systems exist."

repository_evidence.observation: Owns run-persistent `Progress`, `IsOpen`, and a permanently disabled `doorwayBlocker` (set in `Complete()`), with only `StartInteraction`/`CancelInteraction`/`Tick` as public mutators. `CancelInteraction()` clears interaction progress but does not restore `IsOpen` or re-enable the blocker, so no usable reset entry point exists today.

`door-open-interaction.acceptance_criteria` (5 entries) and `encounter-admission-cap-enforcement.acceptance_criteria` (3 entries) contain no reset-entry-point requirement, while `floor-run-restart-bootstrap.depends_on[door-open-interaction]` and `floor-run-restart-persistent-closure.depends_on[encounter-admission-cap-enforcement]` both justify the edge by that missing interface.

finding.recommended_change: Add an owner-side acceptance criterion to `door-open-interaction` requiring an owner-controlled reset entry point that returns its owned opening state (interaction progress, open flag, doorway-blocker enablement) to floor-initial values for consumption by the Floor Run/Restart Orchestrator, referencing GDD §2 Floor-run restart ownership. Add the equivalent criterion to `encounter-admission-cap-enforcement` for encounter activation/admission state. Keep the existing dependency edges — they become correct once the owners are required to produce the interface.

finding.title: Victory capability depends on suspend/re-enable interfaces that Player Movement and Door/Interaction are not required to expose
finding.description:
`final-escape-victory` carries six dependencies, each justified by the consumed owner-controlled gameplay-enable/suspend interface. Three of the five suspend providers (`fireball`, `frost-field`, `force-wave`) each carry an explicit acceptance criterion requiring that interface. The other two do not.

`player-movement`'s acceptance criteria cover mouse-directed movement, the shared pointer target, the movement-restriction request/release interface, and the restart reset entry point — there is no gameplay-enable/suspend criterion, yet `final-escape-victory.depends_on[player-movement]` states "Victory must be able to stop already-active movement through an owner-controlled suspend interface."

`door-open-interaction` likewise has no suspend criterion, yet `final-escape-victory.depends_on[door-open-interaction]` states "Victory must be able to stop an in-progress door approach/opening through an owner-controlled suspend interface."

The GDD makes this an explicit five-owner obligation and an ownership invariant: victory must not reach into movement/door internals, so if the owners are never required to expose suspend/re-enable, the only implementable path for `final-escape-victory` violates the invariant. This is an owner/consumer contract represented only in a consumer's dependency prose.

gdd_evidence.requirement: "Player Movement, Door/Interaction, Fireball, Frost Field, and Force Wave each expose an owner-controlled gameplay-enable/suspend interface that can immediately stop or cancel their current input-driven activity, reject new gameplay commands while suspended, and be re-enabled by an authorized reset/test flow."

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §4 — Development Agent Ownership Invariants (Final escape/victory coordination)
gdd_evidence.requirement: "Player Movement, Door/Interaction, Fireball, Frost Field, and Force Wave remain owners of their own active behavior and must expose owner-controlled suspend/re-enable entry points consumed by victory/reset flows. Final escape logic must not reach into movement, door, or spell internals to stop them."

repository_evidence.observation: `Update()` unconditionally polls `Keyboard.current` and calls `controller.Move(...)`; there is no enable/suspend flag, gating, or public entry point through which an external system could stop active movement.

finding.title: Enemy archetypes must deliver assembled SpriteRenderer prefabs following conventions owned by world-visual-foundation, with no dependency on that owner
finding.description:
`melee-enemy` and `ranged-enemy` each carry an acceptance criterion requiring delivery of "a usable assembled world-space SpriteRenderer archetype prefab", and both cite the GDD's isometric sorting-convention requirement as evidence. The owner of those conventions and of the SpriteRenderer/visual-gameplay separation is `world-visual-foundation` (kind: implementation), which is currently `repository_state: missing`. Neither archetype depends on it.

The GDD explicitly folds character presentation into the reusable visual-world foundation rather than treating it as a separate rendering architecture, so the archetype prefab-assembly criterion cannot be implemented or meaningfully validated against "consistent isometric sorting conventions" before that foundation defines them. Both archetypes are otherwise reachable in the graph once pursuit/health/registry land, which means `taskcontrol ready` can expose prefab-assembly work that will either invent ad-hoc sorting conventions or be reworked when the foundation lands.

The proposed target is `kind: implementation`, so this is a legal edge under the deferred-feature-prerequisite rule (unlike the prohibited `dungeon-encounter-content-authoring -> five-room-content-authoring` edge, which the candidate correctly omits). This is a dependency question only; I am not recommending propagation of `world-visual-foundation`'s builder/scene write locks to the archetypes.

gdd_evidence.requirement: "World-space SpriteRenderer prefabs will be used for sealed doors, tall props, obstacles, the wizard, enemies, and other independently sorted or interactive objects. Character presentation is therefore part of the reusable visual-world foundation rather than a separate rendering architecture."

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §3 — Environment Presentation and Authoring Direction
gdd_evidence.requirement: "Placeholder character sprites are acceptable during development, but the wizard and enemy visual representations follow the same isometric sorting conventions as other world-space SpriteRenderers."

repository_evidence.observation: Per the candidate's own verified evidence, the builder creates Floor/Walls/door visual as primitive meshes with MeshRenderers and creates no SpriteRenderer, Tilemap, or Grid; no isometric sorting convention exists anywhere in the repository for an archetype prefab to follow.

`melee-enemy.acceptance_criteria` and `ranged-enemy.acceptance_criteria` each require "a usable assembled world-space SpriteRenderer archetype prefab" citing "Environment Presentation and Authoring Direction", while `depends_on` lists only `enemy-pursuit-search-foundation`, `enemy-health-damage-defeat`, and `active-enemy-registry`.

finding.recommended_change: Either (a) add `depends_on: world-visual-foundation` to `melee-enemy` and `ranged-enemy`, justified by the SpriteRenderer/isometric-sorting conventions their prefab-delivery criterion consumes; or (b) if the intent is that archetypes ship with placeholder presentation and are re-sorted later, narrow the archetype acceptance criterion so it does not claim conformance to conventions that do not yet exist, and record the presentation conformance as a later obligation on `world-visual-foundation` or on encounter authoring. Do not add `world-visual-foundation`'s builder/scene exclusive-resource locks to the archetypes as part of either option.

finding.title: Two independently approved package configurations are fused into one node, creating a cross-system prerequisite
finding.description:
`tilemap-navigation-package-configuration` bundles `com.unity.2d.tilemap` (the Isometric Tilemap authoring package) and `com.unity.ai.navigation` (the enemy-navigation package). The GDD approves them in separate bullets with separate downstream consumers: the Tilemap package is a prerequisite for the visual authoring workflow, the AI Navigation package is a prerequisite for the navigation/locomotion layer and locomotion-dependent enemy work.

Because both `gameplay-navigation-locomotion` and `world-visual-foundation` depend on the fused node, each is nominally blocked on a package it does not consume. The practical impact is small — both entries land in one `Packages/manifest.json` edit, and fusing them avoids a same-file writer collision — so I am not asserting this is incorrect. It is noted as the one place where the graph's dependency semantics are broader than the underlying GDD prerequisite relationships, in case a later pass wants the navigation package configuration to be independently dispatchable ahead of visual work.

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §5 — Approved Unity Packages and Windows Build Configuration
gdd_evidence.requirement: "Unity 2D Tilemap Editor (com.unity.2d.tilemap) is approved and required for the intended Isometric Tilemap authoring workflow." and separately "Unity AI Navigation (com.unity.ai.navigation) is the approved enemy-navigation implementation. If it is absent from Packages/manifest.json, adding/configuring it is a prerequisite for the gameplay navigation/locomotion layer and locomotion-dependent enemy work."

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD §5 — 2.5D Isometric Visual and World Representation
gdd_evidence.requirement: "A minimal working navigation/locomotion layer and the approved package configuration must exist before locomotion-dependent enemy implementation is dispatched, but room-specific visual authoring does not need to be complete first."

repository_evidence.observation: Neither approved package is declared; both would be added by editing the same single shared manifest file, which is why the fused representation is defensible as a scheduling choice.

finding.recommended_change: Optional. If a later pass wants navigation work to proceed independently of Tilemap authoring readiness, split into two implementation items sharing `repo-file:Packages/manifest.json` as an exclusive resource, and point `gameplay-navigation-locomotion` at the AI Navigation item and `world-visual-foundation` at the Tilemap item. Otherwise leave as-is and treat the extra prerequisite as an accepted simplification.

finding.title: door-open-interaction's potential write to Assets/InputSystem_Actions.inputactions is unresolved but concurrently reachable with three spell tasks that do hold that lock
finding.description: player-movement, fireball, frost-field, and force-wave all correctly carry the repo-file:Assets/InputSystem_Actions.inputactions lock because each is expected to add/modify bindings in that single shared action asset. door-open-interaction also requires cursor-targeted, Input-System-routed door selection (GDD Section 2 'Open Sealed Door'; Section 5 Runtime Implementation) and depends_on player-movement, so it becomes ready at the same point in the graph as fireball/frost-field/force-wave (none of which depend on each other or on door-open-interaction). The candidate itself flags in unresolved_questions that it cannot yet determine whether door-open-interaction must independently add a binding to that asset or will purely consume a Point/Click action that player-movement's work adds. Per the audit's evidence rule, the candidate is correct not to assert the lock without positive write evidence, and it has properly surfaced the ambiguity rather than silently guessing either way. However, this leaves a real (not merely speculative) coverage gap: if door-open-interaction turns out to need its own binding, it can be dispatched concurrently with fireball/frost-field/force-wave without the matching lock, risking an unguarded concurrent write to the shared action asset.

gdd_evidence.reference: GDD Section 2 Player Actions and Systems - Open Sealed Door / Section 5 Runtime Implementation
gdd_evidence.requirement: Door selection/approach input is consumed through the project's Unity Input System/Input Actions layer rather than independent direct hardware polling.

repository_evidence.observation: Stock template asset with no gameplay-map Point/Click or door-select action; whether door-open-interaction adds its own binding here or purely consumes a binding added by player-movement cannot be determined from current repository state.

finding.recommended_change: Resolve the candidate's own unresolved_question before door-open-interaction is dispatched concurrently with fireball/frost-field/force-wave: either (a) confirm door-open-interaction only consumes an existing/soon-to-exist Point/Click binding and add explicit acceptance-criteria language establishing that as the implementation boundary, or (b) add repo-file:Assets/InputSystem_Actions.inputactions to door-open-interaction's exclusive_resources defensively until that boundary is settled.
